Costa Rica’s Chemicals Industry Faces Credit Freeze as Firms Struggle to Stay Solvent

A sudden credit freeze is roiling Costa Rica’s chemicals industry, leaving companies scrambling to secure financing and forcing some to scale back operations as lenders tighten standards. The crisis, which began last week after several mid-sized producers reported difficulties rolling over short-term debt, has already resulted in delayed shipments, production cutbacks and warnings of possible layoffs.

Empaques Universal SA, a major player in the sector, confirmed on Monday that negotiations with its primary bank for a credit line extension had stalled. “We are doing everything possible to keep our commitments to clients while we navigate these unprecedented conditions,” said CEO Rafael Molina. “The lack of liquidity is a daily challenge.”

According to the Costa Rican Chemical Industry Association, more than 60% of local firms now face restricted access to credit, while new lending has nearly ground to a halt. “This is the most severe financing crunch our sector has seen in over a decade,” said Association President Laura Salazar. “Many companies have no choice but to halt investment plans and reduce production.”

Industry analysts attribute the freeze to growing concerns over the sector’s high leverage and weakening foreign demand, which has put pressure on receivables. “Banks have become extremely cautious, increasing collateral demands and shortening repayment terms,” said Andrés Vargas, a chemicals sector analyst at Consultora Soluciones.

Workers’ unions warn that if the credit freeze persists, job losses could follow. “We urge authorities and financial institutions to act urgently,” said union leader Francisco Gómez. “Thousands of livelihoods are at risk.”

As of Tuesday, there was little sign of immediate relief. The government is said to be monitoring the situation, but no concrete measures have been announced. For now, chemical firms in Costa Rica continue to face significant uncertainty.
